stars.label: Consciousness
stars.title: Consciousness
stars.body: There is something it is like to see red or feel a pain. How that comes from a brain, or whether it does, is open. People who study it do not agree on what would count as an answer.

stars.label: The hard problem
stars.title: The hard problem
stars.body: Chalmers (1995) separated the easier questions about how the brain processes information from the harder one of why any of it is felt. Some think the question is real and deep. Others think it will dissolve as the easier ones are answered.

stars.label: The self
stars.title: The self
stars.body: Each of us feels like one thing that lasts through the years. Philosophers ask what makes you the same person as the child in an old photograph, and some traditions, among them Buddhist ones, hold that no fixed self is there to find.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Personal Identity

stars.label: Other minds
stars.title: Other minds
stars.body: You never feel anyone else’s experience, and you still take them to have it. The usual support is that others look and act like you. The same question comes up again for animals and machines.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Other Minds

stars.label: Memory
stars.title: Memory
stars.body: Remembering is a rebuilding. Each time a memory is called up it is put together again, which is why vivid memories can be wrong and why a shared past is so often told differently by the people who were there.

stars.label: Agency
stars.title: Agency
stars.body: The sense of agency is the feeling that you are the one causing what happens. It can be measured, and it can go missing or appear where it should not, which makes it a good place to study how choosing feels from the inside.

stars.label: Free will
stars.title: Free will
stars.body: If the world follows laws, in what sense could you have done otherwise? Some say free will is false. Some say it is compatible with the laws. Some say it needs something the laws leave open. These views are all held by careful people.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Free Will

stars.label: Attention
stars.title: Attention
stars.body: Attention picks a small part of what reaches you and lets the rest fade. It is partly something you do and partly something done to you by a loud noise or a bright thing.

stars.label: Flow
stars.title: Flow
stars.body: Some activities absorb a person so fully that the sense of time and of self recede. Csikszentmihalyi (1990) called this flow and studied it in athletes, artists and surgeons.

stars.label: Mind
stars.title: Mind
stars.body: A way into the mind through what it is like to be aware and what it is to choose. Gödel’s arguments about mind and machine sit next to these questions.

stars.label: Where language began
stars.title: Where language began
stars.body: Nobody knows how or when speech began, because it leaves no fossils. Proposals range from gesture to song to tool making, and the question is studied by linguists, archaeologists and biologists together.

stars.label: Language families
stars.title: Language families
stars.body: Languages that share a common ancestor form a family. Comparing words and sounds across Europe and India led to Indo-European, and similar work has grouped many of the world’s languages.

stars.label: Sign languages
stars.title: Sign languages
stars.body: Sign languages are full languages with their own grammar, and they arise wherever deaf people gather. Nicaraguan Sign Language was born in a school in the 1970s and 80s and is one of the few cases of a new language seen from its beginning.

stars.label: Languages at risk
stars.title: Languages at risk
stars.body: Thousands of languages are spoken by small communities, and many are no longer passed to children. Each one holds a way of naming the world, and communities, linguists and schools work to record and revive them.

stars.label: Grammar
stars.title: Grammar
stars.body: Every language has patterns that speakers follow without being taught the rules. Some linguists look for what all grammars share. Others look at how much they differ.

stars.label: Meaning
stars.title: Meaning
stars.body: What makes a sound or mark mean something? Answers include what the speaker intends, how the word is used, and what it points to in the world. Each fits some cases better than others.

stars.label: Translation
stars.title: Translation
stars.body: No two languages cut the world in the same places, so translating means choosing what to keep. A good translator weighs sound, sense and tone, and two good translations of one poem can differ a lot.

stars.label: Does language shape thought?
stars.title: Does language shape thought?
stars.body: The Sapir-Whorf idea says the language you speak steers how you think. Some experiments, for example with color words and with ways of describing direction, find small effects. Others find none. The strong version is widely doubted.

stars.label: Metaphor
stars.title: Metaphor
stars.body: We talk about time as money and arguments as war, and the talk shapes what we notice. Lakoff and Johnson (1980) argued that metaphor is a main way people think about abstract things.

stars.label: Names
stars.title: Names
stars.body: A name points at one person, place or thing. How it manages that, and what happens when the thing changes, was a long argument in the twentieth century, with Kripke (1972) as a main voice. verify

stars.label: Language
stars.title: Language
stars.body: A way into language through how it is spoken and passed on, and through what words do. Writing sits with History, and Gödel’s trick is a story of a language that learned to talk about itself.

stars.label: Why we tell stories
stars.title: Why we tell stories
stars.body: People in every known society tell stories. They carry memory, teach, entertain and bind a group. Some researchers think the habit helps us rehearse situations before we meet them.

stars.label: The novel
stars.title: The novel
stars.body: The novel took the stories people told for each other and gave them the length to follow one inner life. Don Quixote (1605), The Tale of Genji (about 1000) and many others show the form arriving in different places at different times.

stars.label: Poetry
stars.title: Poetry
stars.body: Poetry packs sound, rhythm and image into few words. Many poems began as songs, and in many cultures the first literature in a language is verse.

stars.label: Plays and performance
stars.title: Plays and performance
stars.body: A story acted in front of people is told in a different way from one read alone. Greek tragedy, Sanskrit drama, Noh and the Yoruba masquerade each grew from their own occasions and audiences.

stars.label: Literature
stars.title: Literature
stars.body: Literature is the writing a community keeps and rereads. Which writing is kept, in which languages, and by whom decided, is an old question and the center of the idea of a canon.

stars.label: Folktales
stars.title: Folktales
stars.body: Tales passed from person to person turn up in forms that resemble each other across many places. Collectors such as the brothers Grimm, and later the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index, gathered them and sorted them into types.

stars.label: Epics
stars.title: Epics
stars.body: Gilgamesh, the Iliad and the Odyssey, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, Sundiata, the Kalevala and the Epic of Manas are long poems that peoples keep as part of their story of who they are.

stars.label: Origin stories
stars.title: Origin stories
stars.body: Peoples everywhere have told how the world and the first people came to be, and these stories differ widely. The Rigveda asks whether even the gods knew, the Popol Vuh tells of Maya creators who tried more than once, and Aboriginal Australian peoples speak of ancestors who made the land while traveling. Each is told by its own people in its own terms, and each can be read next to the others without ranking. verify

stars.label: Stories of a great flood
stars.title: Stories of a great flood
stars.body: A flood that reshapes the world appears in the stories of Mesopotamia, in the Hebrew Bible, in India, in Greece, in Mesoamerica and in many other places. Some scholars study how the accounts relate to each other and to real floods, and communities that hold them keep their own readings. verify

stars.label: Tricksters
stars.title: Tricksters
stars.body: Anansi in West Africa and the Caribbean, Coyote in many North American traditions, Loki in the Norse tales and Hermes in Greece are figures who break rules and make mischief, and through that show where the rules are.

stars.label: Reading traditional stories
stars.title: Reading traditional stories
stars.body: Scholars have read traditional stories as early science, as charters for a way of life, as structures of the mind and as art. For the communities who tell them they are often sacred or true in their own way, and a respectful reading keeps both in view. verify

stars.label: Stories and literature
stars.title: Stories and literature
stars.body: A way into stories through how they are told and written, and through the ones that peoples have kept for ages. Religions and Cultures hold some of the same stories from the inside.

stars.label: The cell
stars.title: The cell
stars.body: Every living thing is made of cells, from one to many trillions. The cell is a small crowded world with walls, machinery and a copy of its own instructions.

stars.label: DNA and heredity
stars.title: DNA and heredity
stars.body: Parents pass instructions to their young in a long chain of four letters. After Watson, Crick, Franklin and others found its shape (1953), reading and copying it became possible.

stars.label: Evolution
stars.title: Evolution
stars.body: Darwin and Wallace (1858, 1859) described how small differences, passed on, and a world where not all can survive lead to the variety of life. It joins the fossils, the genes and the living world in one account.

stars.label: Ecosystems
stars.title: Ecosystems
stars.body: A forest, a reef or a pond is a set of living things and the stuff they trade: food, water, carbon, shelter. Take one part away and others change.

stars.label: Living together
stars.title: Living together
stars.body: Lichens are fungi and algae in one body. Gut bacteria help digest food. Mitochondria in our cells began as separate living things, as Margulis argued in the 1960s. Cooperation runs deep in the history of life.

stars.label: How life began
stars.title: How life began
stars.body: Somewhere on the early Earth chemistry turned into living cells. How exactly, nobody has shown. Warm pools, deep sea vents and clay surfaces are among the places researchers look.

stars.label: Aging and death
stars.title: Aging and death
stars.body: Living things wear, and most die. Biologists ask why aging evolved, and cultures ask what to do with the dead. Both questions are old.

stars.label: Extinction
stars.title: Extinction
stars.body: Most species that ever lived are gone. There have been five great die-offs in the fossil record, and scientists are asking whether human activity has started another.

stars.label: Life
stars.title: Life
stars.body: A way into life through how it works inside a cell and how it plays out across a planet. Mind sits at the far end of the same story.

stars.label: Plate tectonics
stars.title: Plate tectonics
stars.body: The surface of the Earth is made of plates that move a few centimeters a year. They explain mountains, earthquakes and why the same fossils turn up on coasts now far apart. Wegener proposed drifting continents in 1912 and the idea was accepted decades later.

stars.label: Water
stars.title: Water
stars.body: Water covers most of the planet and moves through oceans, air, ice, rivers and living bodies. It shapes where people settle and what they fight over.

stars.label: Climate
stars.title: Climate
stars.body: Climate is the long pattern of weather. Measurements show the planet warming since the nineteenth century because of greenhouse gases from human activity, and the choices about what to do belong to people and their societies.

stars.label: The ocean
stars.title: The ocean
stars.body: The ocean holds most of the planet’s water and most of its living space, and a large part of it has never been seen. It stores heat and carries it around the globe.

stars.label: Deep time
stars.title: Deep time
stars.body: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Layers of rock, read like pages, gave people a way to feel the age. James Hutton and later geologists made it a measurable thing.

stars.label: Cycles of matter
stars.title: Cycles of matter
stars.body: Carbon, nitrogen and other elements move between rock, air, water and living things. A small shift in one cycle, such as the carbon one, can matter on every scale.

stars.label: Ice ages
stars.title: Ice ages
stars.body: For the last two and a half million years the planet has moved between long cold periods and warm ones, paced in part by slow changes in its orbit and tilt.

stars.label: The age of people
stars.title: The age of people
stars.body: Some scientists propose naming a new time in Earth’s history, the Anthropocene, for the mark that humans leave. Others, including the body that sets the official time scale, have declined to adopt it, and some prefer other names or argue that the label hides who is responsible.

stars.label: Earth
stars.title: Earth
stars.body: A way into the planet through its present and its long changes. The sky’s story under Astronomy and the story of living things under Life both stand on it.

stars.label: The state
stars.title: The state
stars.body: A state claims the right to make rules over a territory. How it gets that right, and what limits it, is what political philosophers from Hobbes to Locke to Confucian thinkers argued about in different ways.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Political Philosophy

stars.label: Law
stars.title: Law
stars.body: Law is a set of rules a community backs with force and, at its best, with reasons. People ask whether a rule that is unjust is still law, and traditions answer differently.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Philosophy of Law

stars.label: Power
stars.title: Power
stars.body: Power is the ability to make others act. It can rest on force, on money, on the consent of those ruled or on the stories a society tells itself. Gödel’s worry about a rule set that can be bent from inside belongs here.

stars.label: Voting and democracy
stars.title: Voting and democracy
stars.body: Democracy began in forms such as Athenian assemblies and many village councils around the world. Modern versions use elections and courts, and each design trades something away: speed, fairness, protection for minorities.

stars.label: Exchange
stars.title: Exchange
stars.body: People have traded since long before money. Markets, gifts and sharing within a family are different ways to pass things between people, and every society mixes them in its own way.

stars.label: Trust and cooperation
stars.title: Trust and cooperation
stars.body: Groups work when people can count on each other. Trust is built through repeated dealings, shared norms and institutions that make cheating costly. It breaks faster than it builds.

stars.label: The commons
stars.title: The commons
stars.body: Some things belong to everyone: a pasture, a fishery, a language, an internet. Hardin warned in 1968 that shared things get overused. Ostrom showed in her work that many communities have governed a commons well for centuries, and shared the 2009 economics prize for it.

stars.label: Cities
stars.title: Cities
stars.body: Cities put more people together than any village could. They grew along rivers and trade routes and became places where ideas, goods and diseases pass quickly.

stars.label: Fairness between people
stars.title: Fairness between people
stars.body: Societies differ in how they share what they produce. People disagree about what is fair: equal shares, shares by effort, shares by need. The views sit side by side in the study of justice.

stars.label: Society
stars.title: Society
stars.body: A way into society through how rules and power work and how people live together. Gödel’s ideas about systems and their outside meet this topic in a few places.

stars.label: What is good?
stars.title: What is good?
stars.body: Ethics asks what makes an act right or a life good. It is among the oldest questions and every culture has its own answers, often tied to its stories and its traditions.

stars.label: Three ways to ask
stars.title: Three ways to ask
stars.body: One way looks at outcomes and asks what does the most good. One looks at duties and asks what rules we must keep. One looks at character and asks what a good person would do. Each catches something the other two miss.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Virtue Ethics

stars.label: Do values differ?
stars.title: Do values differ?
stars.body: Moral codes differ across places and times. Some conclude that no view is better than another. Others say that some values, such as care for children, are shared widely, and that argument across differences is possible. The question is still open.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Moral Relativism

stars.label: Justice
stars.title: Justice
stars.body: Justice asks what people are owed. Plato, Aristotle, Confucius and Rawls (1971) each gave an account, and the accounts disagree about whether it is about fair shares, fair process or a harmony of the whole.

stars.label: Rights
stars.title: Rights
stars.body: A right is a claim a person holds that others must respect. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set out a list that many states signed. People still ask where rights come from and which ones count.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

stars.label: Animals
stars.title: Animals
stars.body: Do we owe something to animals, and how much? Views range from care for each animal’s welfare to respect for their lives as such, and traditions around the world have rules about hunting, farming and kinship with other species.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Moral Status of Animals

stars.label: People not yet born
stars.title: People not yet born
stars.body: What do we owe those who come after us? Decisions about the climate, nuclear waste and new technology bind people who cannot take part. Several Indigenous traditions speak of thinking seven generations ahead. verify

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Intergenerational Justice

stars.label: Meaning in life
stars.title: Meaning in life
stars.body: People have answered what makes a life meaningful in many ways: serving a god, loving others, making something that lasts, understanding the world, or accepting that nothing is given and making it up. These stand side by side here.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Meaning of Life

stars.label: Ethics and meaning
stars.title: Ethics and meaning
stars.body: A way into ethics through how to ask what is good and what we owe each other. Religions and Cultures give many of their own answers.

stars.label: Tools
stars.title: Tools
stars.body: Stone tools are at least 3 million years old, older than our species. Making them required planning and passing skill from person to person, and tools changed those who used them.

stars.label: Fire and cooking
stars.title: Fire and cooking
stars.body: Controlled fire gave warmth, light and cooked food. When it began is debated, with evidence of use going back at least hundreds of thousands of years.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Control of fire by early humans

stars.label: Printing
stars.title: Printing
stars.body: Printing with movable type appeared in China and Korea, and Gutenberg’s press in Europe (about 1450) made books cheap. Ideas then traveled faster than the people who held them.

stars.label: Energy
stars.title: Energy
stars.body: Human societies run on energy: muscle, wood, water, coal, oil, sun and wind. Each new source has changed what people could build and where they could live.

stars.label: Computers
stars.title: Computers
stars.body: A computer carries out recipes. Turing and others made precise what that can mean, and the same limits that Gödel found show up in what programs can decide.

stars.label: The internet
stars.title: The internet
stars.body: A network of networks joined in the late twentieth century. It made it possible to reach nearly any written thing from nearly anywhere, and also to be reached.

stars.label: Artificial intelligence
stars.title: Artificial intelligence
stars.body: Programs now write, draw, translate and play. Whether they understand anything, whether they could be conscious and how to keep them safe are open questions, and Gödel’s results are often cited in the debate.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Artificial Intelligence

stars.label: Making things safe
stars.title: Making things safe
stars.body: Bridges, aircraft and medicines are tested and made to fail gently. The same idea of building the check into the system is now applied to software that learns.

stars.label: Who decides?
stars.title: Who decides?
stars.body: Tools serve whoever holds them. Questions about who builds new technology, who controls it and who bears its harm belong to ethics and society as much as to engineering.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Philosophy of Technology

stars.label: Technology
stars.title: Technology
stars.body: A way into technology through how things are made and how thinking machines arrived. Math and Time sit underneath it.

stars.label: Why make art?
stars.title: Why make art?
stars.body: The oldest known cave paintings are tens of thousands of years old. Across the world people have made images, songs and ornaments for ritual, memory, beauty, play and to say what words could not.

stars.label: Craft
stars.title: Craft
stars.body: Weaving, pottery, carving and metalwork are skills handed down over generations. Many cultures do not separate craft and art, and a well made cup can be both.

stars.label: Dance
stars.title: Dance
stars.body: Dance shapes time and space with the body. It is part of rituals, courtship and celebration in nearly every society.

stars.label: Film
stars.title: Film
stars.body: Moving images turned a century ago into a main way stories are told. Montage, the joining of shots, gave cinema its own grammar.

stars.label: Architecture
stars.title: Architecture
stars.body: Buildings shelter and also say something: about power, belief, community. The same need produces a tent, a temple and a tower in different places.

stars.label: Beauty
stars.title: Beauty
stars.body: People call things beautiful across every culture and disagree about what that means. Some say beauty lies in the thing, some in the eye, some in a shared practice of looking.

stars.label: Perspective
stars.title: Perspective
stars.body: Renaissance painters in Italy worked out how to draw depth with geometry, and the method spread. Other traditions, such as Chinese scroll painting and Mughal miniatures, solve the same problem with different tools.

stars.label: Color
stars.title: Color
stars.body: Color is made in the eye and brain from light of different wavelengths. Peoples name colors in different numbers of groups, and pigments have their own history of trade and discovery.

stars.label: Copying and owning
stars.title: Copying and owning
stars.body: Artists have always learned by copying. Laws on who owns a picture, a song or an idea changed with printing and again with the internet, and there are still conflicting views on where to draw the line.

stars.label: Many traditions
stars.title: Many traditions
stars.body: Most people alive belong to a religious tradition, and the traditions differ a great deal in what they hold, how they gather and what they ask of a person. A fair account describes each one as its followers would, and lets readers compare without ranking.

sources.t: Wikipedia: List of religions and spiritual traditions

stars.label: Hinduism
stars.title: Hinduism
stars.body: Hinduism is a family of traditions from the Indian subcontinent with many gods, many paths and a large body of texts, among them the Vedas, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita. Many Hindus hold ideas of dharma, karma, rebirth and liberation (moksha), and they differ on how these are understood.

stars.label: Buddhism
stars.title: Buddhism
stars.body: Buddhism began with the teaching of the Buddha in northern India about 2,500 years ago. It holds that suffering has a cause and an end and describes a path to it. It has several schools, Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana among them, and ways of practice from silent sitting to chanting.

stars.label: Judaism
stars.title: Judaism
stars.body: Judaism holds a covenant between God and the people of Israel, with the Torah at its center and a long tradition of study and commentary. Observance and belief vary among Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and other communities, and among secular Jews who keep the culture.

stars.label: Christianity
stars.title: Christianity
stars.body: Christianity centers on the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth as the New Testament tells it. It includes Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches and many others, which differ in worship, authority and teaching.

stars.label: Islam
stars.title: Islam
stars.body: Muslims hold that God revealed the Quran to the prophet Muhammad in the seventh century. Five pillars shape practice: the declaration of faith, prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca. The main branches are Sunni and Shia, and Sufi paths run through both.

stars.label: Sikhism
stars.title: Sikhism
stars.body: Sikhism began in the Punjab with Guru Nanak and nine Gurus after him. It teaches one God, honest work, sharing with others and service. The Guru Granth Sahib is its scripture and is treated as the living guide.

stars.label: Daoism
stars.title: Daoism
stars.body: Daoism draws on the Dao De Jing, attributed to Laozi, and the Zhuangzi, which speak of following the way of the world. It grew into a tradition with temples, priests, meditation and ritual, and it shaped Chinese life with Buddhism and Confucian thought.

stars.label: Confucian tradition
stars.title: Confucian tradition
stars.body: Confucius (551 to 479 BCE) taught virtue, family duty and learning, and later thinkers built a tradition on it that shaped East Asian states and homes. Whether it is a religion, an ethic or both is debated, and its followers answer differently. verify

stars.label: Jainism
stars.title: Jainism
stars.body: Jainism teaches non-violence (ahimsa) toward all living things and holds that each soul can free itself by its own effort. Its line of teachers includes Mahavira, who lived in India about the same time as the Buddha. verify

stars.label: Shinto
stars.title: Shinto
stars.body: Shinto is the Japanese tradition of kami, the spirits present in places, ancestors and natural things. Its shrines, festivals and rites of purity are part of everyday and seasonal life in Japan.

stars.label: Baháʼí Faith
stars.title: Baháʼí Faith
stars.body: The Baháʼí Faith began in nineteenth century Persia with Baháʼu’lláh. Its followers hold the unity of God, of religion and of humanity, and they gather in many countries. verify

stars.label: Indigenous spiritual traditions
stars.title: Indigenous spiritual traditions
stars.body: Indigenous peoples hold many different spiritual traditions, each tied to a land, a language and a community. Many speak of the land, the sky, animals and ancestors as relatives. These traditions speak for themselves, and the Cultures topic holds more about how peoples see the cosmos. verify

stars.label: Sacred texts
stars.title: Sacred texts
stars.body: The Vedas, the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, the Quran, the Pali Canon and the Guru Granth Sahib are texts that communities treat as sacred. Many traditions also hold teachings that were passed on by mouth for a long time before and after writing.

stars.label: Ritual and prayer
stars.title: Ritual and prayer
stars.body: Prayer, song, fasting, offerings and silence are ways that people in nearly every tradition mark what matters to them. Rituals also hold communities together through births, marriages and deaths.

stars.label: Pilgrimage
stars.title: Pilgrimage
stars.body: Millions travel each year to places they hold holy: Mecca, Varanasi, Bodh Gaya, Jerusalem, Amritsar, the Camino to Santiago, Ise. The journey itself is part of the practice.

stars.label: Mystical experience
stars.title: Mystical experience
stars.body: People in many traditions describe moments of direct experience of something beyond the ordinary. William James (1902) gathered accounts, and researchers and believers read them in different ways.

sources.t: Wikipedia: The Varieties of Religious Experience

stars.label: Religion and science
stars.title: Religion and science
stars.body: Some people see conflict between them, some see separate questions that need not meet, and some see dialogue or support. Each view has careful defenders on both the religious and the scientific side.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Religion and Science

stars.label: Living without religion
stars.title: Living without religion
stars.body: Many people hold no religion, among them atheists, agnostics, humanists and those who are unsure. They live by their own sources of meaning, and many value what religious traditions pass on.

stars.label: Freedom of belief
stars.title: Freedom of belief
stars.body: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) sets out the right to hold a belief, to change it and to practice it with others. How far it reaches is argued in many countries.

stars.label: Dialogue between traditions
stars.title: Dialogue between traditions
stars.body: People of different traditions meet to learn, to work together and to disagree with respect. Some of it is formal, as in interfaith councils. Much of it happens in neighborhoods.

stars.label: Religions
stars.title: Religions
stars.body: A way into the world’s religions and spiritual paths, each in its own words and none ranked. People who hold a tradition are invited to improve what is written about it. Where views differ they sit side by side.

stars.label: What a culture is
stars.title: What a culture is
stars.body: A culture is the shared ways of a people: language, customs, beliefs, tools, food and stories. Cultures change as people meet and as generations pass, and no person belongs to only one.

stars.label: Kinship and family
stars.title: Kinship and family
stars.body: Who counts as family, whom one may marry and what relatives owe each other differ widely. Anthropologists found that kinship is organized in a few main patterns but filled in very differently.

stars.label: Food and feasting
stars.title: Food and feasting
stars.body: What people eat, with whom and on what occasion carries meaning. Feasts mark weddings, harvests, mourning and welcome, and recipes travel with people.

stars.label: Rites of passage
stars.title: Rites of passage
stars.body: Van Gennep (1909) noted that societies mark changes in a life, such as birth, adulthood, marriage and death, with rites that separate, transform and reunite a person with the group.

stars.label: Cosmovisions
stars.title: Cosmovisions
stars.body: A cosmovision is the way a people sees the order of the world: land, sky, time, other beings and the place of people among them. Andean, Aboriginal Australian, Māori and many other peoples each hold their own, and they are best learned from the people who live them. verify

stars.label: Indigenous knowledge
stars.title: Indigenous knowledge
stars.body: Peoples who have lived in a place for generations hold detailed knowledge of its plants, animals, weather and seasons. Examples include fire management in Australia, wayfinding across the Pacific without instruments and terraced farming in the Andes. Scientists increasingly work with it as equal knowledge.

stars.label: Music of many peoples
stars.title: Music of many peoples
stars.body: Every culture has music, and each tunes, counts and gathers around it in its own way. The Music topic has gamelan, raga, maqam and drumming from Africa and the Andes among its ideas.

stars.label: Contact and exchange
stars.title: Contact and exchange
stars.body: Peoples have always traded goods, words and ideas. The Silk Road, the Indian Ocean routes and the Atlantic crossings carried spices, crops, religions and numbers, and also disease and conquest.

stars.label: Migration and diaspora
stars.title: Migration and diaspora
stars.body: People move for work, for safety and for love. Communities spread across the world keep ties to a homeland and build new ones where they live.

stars.label: Colonial history
stars.title: Colonial history
stars.body: Many peoples lived under colonial rule that redrew borders, moved populations and suppressed languages and beliefs. Many communities now teach their own history, revive their languages and ask for the return of what was taken.

stars.label: Heritage and return
stars.title: Heritage and return
stars.body: Museums and archives hold objects and records from many peoples. UNESCO lists places and living practices as heritage, and communities and museums negotiate over who should keep what and in what way.

stars.label: Understanding on its own terms
stars.title: Understanding on its own terms
stars.body: Anthropologists learned to describe a way of life as its members do, before judging it. Some then argued that no culture can be judged from outside. Others say some judgments hold across cultures. Both views have careful defenders.

stars.label: Language and belonging
stars.title: Language and belonging
stars.body: A language carries songs, jokes, names for places and ways to address elders. People who lose their language often lose a way of belonging with it, and many communities now teach it to children again.

stars.label: Cultures
stars.title: Cultures
stars.body: A way into cultures through how people live and how they meet and keep what they hold. Each people speaks for itself, and no way of living is a standard for the others.

stars.label: Art
stars.title: Art
stars.body: A way into art through making and through seeing. Music has its own topic and shares many of the same questions.
